inputs.question: In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?
inputs.scope:
Covers: Interventions delivered in low- and middle-income countries that aim to improve educational outcomes for children and young people with disabilities. Outcomes include enrolment, attendance, retention, completion, learning or achievement, and school participation. It also covers the comparative effectiveness of programme types: school-based inclusion, teacher training, assistive devices, accessibility changes, community and family-based approaches, financial incentives, and specialised provision.
Out of scope:
- Effectiveness of disability-inclusive education in high-income countries (The question is restricted to LMICs, and contexts, resources and systems differ substantially.)
- Health or rehabilitation outcomes (e.g. functional improvement, vision correction) that are not linked to education outcomes (The question asks about education, so clinical effects count only if they translate into schooling or learning outcomes.)
- Prevalence of disability and the size of the education gap for children with disabilities (This is descriptive context, not whether programmes work.)
- Whether inclusive education is a rights obligation under the CRPD (This is a normative and legal question, not an empirical effectiveness one.)
- Effects of inclusion on non-disabled classmates (The question concerns outcomes for children and young people with disabilities.)
- Cost-effectiveness and financing comparisons (These need cost data beyond effectiveness evidence and would be a separate analysis.)
inputs.judgement: All but one study received an overall rating of low confidence in study findings.
